new_d.text: Deleuze and Guattari's model of thought and organization, set out in the introduction to A Thousand Plateaus: a network in which any point can connect to any other, with no root, center or fixed order, always in the middle.

new_text.text: A rhizome as subterranean stem, the authors write, is absolutely different from roots and radicles; bulbs and tubers are rhizomes, and so are rats and burrows, potato and couchgrass (pp. 6–7).

Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975) already calls Kafka's work a rhizome, a burrow with many entrances, none of them privileged, and A Thousand Plateaus calls the burrow an animal rhizome with multiple entryways (p. 12).
Pages of A Thousand Plateaus are from Brian Massumi's translation (1987).

Against the rhizome stands the tree, the arborescent model of thought, which “plots a point, fixes an order” (p. 7), as the linguistic tree of Chomsky's model begins at a point and proceeds by dichotomy (p. 7).

The tree, in the authors' words, is filiation, and the rhizome “uniquely alliance”; the tree imposes the verb “to be”, and the fabric of the rhizome is the conjunction “and . . . and . . . and . . .” (p. 25).
The introduction enumerates “certain approximate characteristics of the rhizome” (p. 7).

By the principles of connection and heterogeneity, “any point of a rhizome can be connected to anything other, and must be” (p. 7); by the principle of multiplicity, the multiple treated as a substantive ceases to have any relation to the One as subject or object (p. 8); and by the principle of asignifying rupture, a rhizome shattered at a given spot starts up again on one of its old lines or on new ones (p. 8).

In the authors' example the wasp and the orchid form a rhizome through “a capture of code”, a becoming-wasp of the orchid and a becoming-orchid of the wasp (p. 10); the orchid, they write, “forms a map with the wasp, in a rhizome” (p. 12).
By the principles of cartography and decalcomania a rhizome is “a stranger to any idea of genetic axis or deep structure” (p. 12).
The authors call genetic axis and deep structure principles of tracing, and find tree logic, a logic of tracing and reproduction, in linguistics as in psychoanalysis (p. 12).
The map is “open and connectable in all of its dimensions”, detachable, reversible and susceptible to constant modification (p. 12).
A later summary calls the rhizome an antigenealogy and an antimemory, and an acentered, nonhierarchical, nonsignifying system defined solely by a circulation of states (p. 21).

The book follows suit: a plateau is any multiplicity connected to others by superficial underground stems so as to form or extend a rhizome (p. 22), and the Authors' Note says the plateaus may be read independently of one another “to a certain extent”, except the conclusion, which should be read at the end (p. xx).
The Stanford Encyclopedia article describes the plateaus as planes of intensity, a rhizome allowing immediate connections between any of its points.

Guides include Brent Adkins's Deleuze and Guattari's A Thousand Plateaus: A Critical Introduction and Guide (2015) and The Deleuze and Guattari Dictionary (2013) by Eugene Young, Gary Genosko and Janell Watson.

new_d.text: Deleuze and Guattari's term, in A Thousand Plateaus, for an arrangement of heterogeneous elements, bodies and statements alike, that holds together for a time and produces effects; developed into a social ontology by Manuel DeLanda.

new_text.text: “Assemblage” is the usual English rendering of the French agencement, a translation the sociologist John Law calls awkward.

Martin Müller and Carolin Schurr describe assemblages as relations among heterogeneous entities working together for a time, and note that Deleuze and Guattari's vocabulary of contagions and epidemics hints at their fluidity and ephemerality.
Pages of A Thousand Plateaus are from Brian Massumi's translation (1987).
The introduction to A Thousand Plateaus calls an assemblage “this increase in the dimensions of a multiplicity”, which changes in nature as it expands its connections (p. 8).
The fourth plateau, “November 20, 1923: Postulates of Linguistics”, gives it two axes (p. 88).

On the horizontal axis it has a segment of content, a machinic assemblage of bodies, of actions and passions, and a segment of expression, a collective assemblage of enunciation, of acts, statements and incorporeal transformations attributed to bodies; on the vertical axis it has territorial or reterritorialized sides, which stabilize it, and “cutting edges of deterritorialization, which carry it away” (p. 88).

One of the authors' examples is feudalism: the bodies of earth, lord, vassal, serf, knight and horse, the oaths and heraldry, the feudal territorialities and the line of deterritorialization that carries away knight and mount (p. 89).

The conclusion adds: “Every assemblage is basically territorial” (p. 503), and its first concrete rule is to discover the territoriality an assemblage envelops (p. 503); the territory, the authors write, makes the assemblage (p. 504).
Assemblages are also passional, “compositions of desire” (p. 399).

The Stanford Encyclopedia article describes the assemblage in A Thousand Plateaus as “an emergent unity joining together heterogeneous bodies in a ‘consistency’”: coding orders matter as it enters a body, stratification makes hierarchies of bodies, and territorialization orders bodies into assemblages.
Lines of flight, in Müller and Schurr's account, take an assemblage apart.

Manuel DeLanda developed the concept into a social ontology in A New Philosophy of Society (2006) and Assemblage Theory (2016), after reconstructing Deleuze's ontology in Intensive Science and Virtual Philosophy (2002).
He takes “relations of exteriority as the defining characteristic of assemblages”: their components are never fully determined by their relations, which lets them plug into other assemblages.
Müller and Schurr find his account “strongly wedded to discrete notions of scales”.

Actor-network theory, associated with Bruno Latour, John Law and Michel Callon, is the neighboring program, and Jane Bennett's Vibrant Matter (2010), in Müller and Schurr's words, “segues between Latour, Deleuze and Guattari”.

Jasbir Puar, who argued in Terrorist Assemblages (2007) that intersectionality must be supplemented by a notion of assemblage, wrote in 2011 that the relation between the two is “frictional”, and that what interests her is what assemblages do.

new_d.text: Deleuze and Guattari's terms for the movement by which something leaves a territory, a code or a habit, and the movement by which it forms a new territory elsewhere.

new_text.text: In Anti-Oedipus the socius has always had to code the flows of desire, and the capitalist machine, built on the ruins of a despotic State, is faced with the task of “decoding and deterritorializing the flows” (p. 33); this, the authors write, is capitalism's most characteristic tendency (p. 34).

Their recapitulation of the three social machines has the despotic machine effect “the first great movement of deterritorialization” by overcoding the territorial communes on the full body of the despot, and the capitalist machine the second, by decoding the flows on the full body of capital-money; capitalism reterritorializes where it has lost the territorialities (p. 261).
What modern societies deterritorialize with one hand, the authors write, they reterritorialize with the other, on neoterritorialities that are often artificial, residual or archaic (p. 257).
Pages of Anti-Oedipus are from the translation by Robert Hurley, Mark Seem and Helen R. Lane (1977).
For A Thousand Plateaus the Stanford Encyclopedia article glosses deterritorialization as the breaking of habits and reterritorialization as their formation.
The book's seventh plateau states the first theorem of deterritorialization: “One never deterritorializes alone” (p. 174).

There are always at least two terms, hand and object of use, mouth and breast, face and landscape, each reterritorializing on the other, and reterritorialization works by artifice: one element, itself deterritorialized, serves as a new territoriality for another that has lost its own (p. 174).
Pages of A Thousand Plateaus are from Brian Massumi's translation (1987).

The third plateau, “10,000 B.C.: The Geology of Morals”, makes absolute deterritorialization primary: it becomes relative only once strata form on the plane of consistency or body without organs, and it is perpetually immanent in relative deterritorialization (p. 56).
The conclusion calls deterritorialization the movement by which one leaves the territory, “the operation of the line of flight” (p. 508), and sorts its cases (pp. 508–510).

It is negative when a compensatory reterritorialization obstructs the line of flight, as the State apparatus reterritorializes on property, work and money; positive but relative when it prevails over its reterritorializations while its line of flight is segmented or sinks into black holes; and absolute when it creates a new earth, connecting lines of flight or drawing a plane of consistency; the authors count at least four forms in all (pp. 508–510).

“Absolute” names a type of movement qualitatively different from relative movement and expresses nothing transcendent, so absolute deterritorialization proceeds by way of relative deterritorialization (pp. 509–510).

The eleventh plateau, “1837: Of the Refrain”, finds three aspects in the refrain: a child in the dark comforting himself with a song, a circle drawn around that fragile center, which makes a home, and the opening of that circle to launch forth (pp. 311–312).

The refrain, the authors write, is rhythm and melody territorialized because they have become expressive (p. 317), and the tenth plateau holds that there is no deterritorialization without a special reterritorialization (p. 303).
Consistency, in the fifth plateau, is deterritorializing (p. 144), and the Stanford article notes that continual deterritorialization is what the authors call consistency.
Language can be deterritorialized too: in Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975) the German of Prague's Jewish writers has a strong coefficient of deterritorialization.

Sara De Balsi sets out the two paths the authors see: a symbolic reterritorialization, which they find in Max Brod, and an absolute deterritorialization, the path of minor literature, Kafka's use of Prague German in its very poverty.

The Stanford article classes deterritorialization among philosophy's concepts, which the authors keep apart in kind from the functions of science, and notes that they repeatedly insist such concepts are no metaphors.

In Anti-Oedipus the authors ask which path is revolutionary, and propose going still further in the movement of the market, of decoding and deterritorialization (p. 239), to “‘accelerate the process,’ as Nietzsche put it” (p. 240); Alex Williams notes that Nick Land later answered this question in the affirmative, while Deleuze and Guattari counseled caution.

new_d.text: In Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975), the literature a minority makes within a major language, marked by the deterritorialization of language, an immediate political charge and a collective value.

new_text.text: Deleuze and Guattari define a minor literature as “the literature a minority makes in a major language”, and their case is Franz Kafka, a Jew in Prague writing in German.

They give it three characteristics: its language has a strong coefficient of deterritorialization; everything in it is political, since in its narrow space every individual matter is plugged straight into politics; and everything in it has a collective value.
Together these, they write, describe the revolutionary conditions of any literature within the great or established one.
Kafka's own word, Sara De Balsi notes, is small (petites littératures in French), and the adjective mineure comes from Marthe Robert's 1954 translation of his diaries.

The authors see two responses to a deterritorialized language: a symbolic reterritorialization, which they find in the Prague school around Max Brod, whose politics ends in the dream of Zion, and an absolute deterritorialization, the path of minor literature, which takes Prague German as it is, in its very poverty.
Joyce, in De Balsi's account of their reading, works by exuberance and overdetermination.
A minor use of language makes a writer a stranger in their own language.
De Balsi holds that only some writers in a second language make a minor literature, and treats it as one possible path for translingual writing.
A Thousand Plateaus returns to the minor in its fourth plateau.

Minor languages exist only in relation to a major language, which they invest in order to make it minor (p. 105), and the authors characterize them here by “a sobriety and variation”, a becoming-minor of the major language (p. 104).

The same page counts the German of Prague among minor languages and reads its alleged poverty as “a restriction of constants” and its overload as “an extension of variations” (p. 104), and minor authors, Deleuze and Guattari write, are foreigners in their own tongue (p. 105).

Majority implies a constant serving as a standard measure, and the minority is “the becoming of everybody” (p. 105); continuous variation, they write, constitutes the becoming-minoritarian of everybody (p. 106).
The same plateau sets minor sciences against the royal or major science of Euclid's invariants (p. 109), and the twelfth plateau speaks of a nomad or minor science (p. 361).
Pages of A Thousand Plateaus are from Brian Massumi's translation (1987).

body-without-organs.old: There the body without organs is the enemy of the organism, a stratum that organizes the organs, and the Stanford article glosses it as “the reservoir of potentials for different patterns of bodily affect”.
body-without-organs.new: There, the authors write, “The enemy is the organism” (p. 158), the organization of the organs, which is a stratum on the body without organs (p. 159), and the Stanford article glosses the body without organs as “the reservoir of potentials for different patterns of bodily affect”.
body-without-organs.note: The book makes the organism the enemy (p. 158) and calls it a stratum on the body without organs (p. 159); the old sentence was ambiguous (its appositive could be read as describing the body without organs) and gave no pages.

body-without-organs.old: The authors treat it as a practice and an experiment, and warn that wild destratification leaves emptied bodies or totalitarian and fascist ones.
body-without-organs.new: The authors call it “a practice, a set of practices” (p. 150) and an experimentation (p. 149), warn that wild destratification leaves emptied bodies (pp. 160–161), and ask how to tell it from its doubles, empty bodies and cancerous, totalitarian and fascist ones (pp. 163, 165).
body-without-organs.note: Wild destratification leaves emptied bodies (pp. 160–161); the cancerous, totalitarian and fascist bodies come from the proliferation of a stratum, the other danger the book names (pp. 163, 165).

coding-decoding.old: A Thousand Plateaus continues this history: the Stanford article describes the state as an “apparatus of capture” “living vampirically off of labor”, a sign of the authors' basically Marxist perspective, and the war machine as the form that “reterritorializes on deterritorialization itself”.
coding-decoding.new: A Thousand Plateaus continues this history in its thirteenth plateau, “7000 B.C.: Apparatus of Capture”, where, following the Marxist description, a State apparatus is erected on primitive agricultural communities and overcodes their lineal-territorial codes (pp. 427–428); the Stanford article reads the state there as an “apparatus of capture” “living vampirically off of labor”, a sign of the authors' basically Marxist perspective. In the twelfth plateau it is the nomad who “reterritorializes on deterritorialization itself” (p. 381); the Stanford article says this of the war machine.
coding-decoding.note: The book says the nomad reterritorializes on deterritorialization itself (p. 381); the Stanford article gives the phrase to the war machine. 'Vampirically' is the article's word, not the book's.
coding-decoding.fix: the book's overcoding passage added; the nomad credited as in the book

summary: Five glossary entries read in A Thousand Plateaus: page numbers throughout; Rhizome and Deterritorialization rebuilt from the book (the Authors' Note's 'to a certain extent' replaces 'in any order'; negative, relative and absolute deterritorialization from the conclusion; Anti-Oedipus credited for what it says); Assemblage gains the book's two axes, unverified before; Plane of immanence and Minor literature gain their A Thousand Plateaus passages, the rest kept for want of What Is Philosophy? and the Kafka book. In Body without organs the two dangers of destratification are kept apart; in Coding, overcoding, decoding the book gives reterritorializing on deterritorialization itself to the nomad (p. 381), the Stanford article to the war machine.

new_d.text: In What Is Philosophy? (1991), the field on which a philosophy creates its concepts; each philosopher, Deleuze and Guattari hold, must lay out a plane of their own.

new_text.text: What Is Philosophy? (1991), the final collaboration between Deleuze and Guattari, calls philosophy “the art of forming, inventing, and fabricating concepts”; science creates functions on a plane of reference, and art creates compounds of percepts and affects, blocs of sensation.
“Thought, in all its modes,” the Stanford article adds, “struggles with chaos against opinion.”

A concept, on the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's account, is an assemblage of components that must stay coherent with one another, a multiplicity, distinct from a proposition, and it “has no relationship to truth, which is an external determination”.
Concepts exist on the plane of immanence, and each philosopher must create such a plane.
The question of what thought presupposes, the IEP notes, is the one Difference and Repetition had treated under the image of thought.
Conceptual personae are “the figures of thought that give concepts their specific force”, and the IEP names the Idiot as Descartes's implicit persona.
“A conceptual persona is not a subject,” the Stanford article explains, “for thinking is not subjective.”
The plane of immanence is opposed to transcendence, and the IEP explains that insisting that immanence be immanent to something is what brings transcendence back and arrests thought.
For Deleuze, the Stanford article notes, Spinoza was the “prince” or even the “Christ” of philosophers, and Deleuze's essay “Immanence: A Life” returns to the theme.
A Thousand Plateaus already speaks of a plane of immanence.

Its tenth plateau, in the sections it calls “Memories of a Spinozist”, describes a fixed plane on which things are distinguished only by speed and slowness, “a plane of immanence or univocality opposed to analogy” (pp. 253–254).

The authors call it the plane of consistency or composition, as opposed to the plan(e) of organization or development, and “necessarily a plane of immanence and univocality”; on it there is no distinction between the natural and the artificial, and it never has a dimension supplementary to what happens on it (p. 266).
The plane of organization and development they call the plane of transcendence (p. 281).
Pages of A Thousand Plateaus are from Brian Massumi's translation (1987).

In its account of What Is Philosophy?, the Stanford article says philosophy gives consistency to the virtual, mapping the forces of a system as pure potentials, while science tracks how the virtual is actualized and explains why one road was taken.
